title: EdTech, AI, and Teaching Series Part 4 Direct Instruction Still Matters
author: Kara Andy
summary: Direct instruction based on Rosenshine's Principles remains essential as AI enters classrooms; AI supports or undermines instructional principles depending on implementation. The key risk is premature AI placement—asking students to generate before understanding foundational concepts leads to shallow strategies. AI strengthens specific phases (explanation with worked examples, checking understanding via hinge questions, guided practice scaffolding) without replacing the teacher. Teachers must maintain boundaries: AI improves thinking rather than replacing it, clarifies rather than completes.
points: Direct instruction—clear goals, explicit modeling, small steps, frequent checking, guided practice, review—remains foundation for effective AI integration.
Minimally guided instruction is ineffective for novices because it overloads working memory; AI amplifies this risk when explicit instruction is weak.
AI should support specific phases: generating worked examples, creating diagnostic prompts, scaffolding practice with guiding questions that prompt revision.
Guided practice is teacher-led where students show mastery before independence; AI should not collapse this boundary by enabling premature independence.
Teachers must teach norms: AI clarifies understanding but doesn't generate answers, supports revision but doesn't replace effort, prompts questions rather than avoiding them.
quotes: As AI becomes visible in classrooms, will it replace direct instruction? The answer, grounded firmly in research, is no—AI makes explicit instruction more important.” “Rosenshine's Principles emphasize that novice learners benefit most when teachers clarify goals, model explicitly, present small steps, check frequently, guide practice, and review.
A common misstep is asking students to generate before understanding underlying concepts; minimally guided instruction overloads working memory and encourages shallow strategies.
When aligned intentionally, AI strengthens instructional practices without replacing the teacher; AI should follow explanation, not replace it—the teacher remains primary model.

Even with AI support, guided practice isn't automated; teachers must circulate, observe, ask questions, and decide when to reteach—AI cannot replace instructional judgment.” Archived from Brewing Innovation Substack on April 21, 2026 by Tim.
